What Is Arbitrariness? Conceptual Definitions and Their Operation in Legal Review of Adjudicators and Decision-Makers

Arbitrariness is not one concept but a family of them, and courts and scholars routinely slide among them without noticing. This report maps eight distinct conceptions — unreasoned decision-making (State Farm, Vavilov), failed means-ends rationality (Bedford, Indian Article 14), inconsistency across adjudicators (Refugee Roulette), unconstrained will (Dicey, Hayek, Raz, void-for-vagueness), republican domination (Pettit, Lovett), procedural unfairness, randomness (Furman, and the lottery literature that defends it), and hybrids including algorithmic arbitrariness. It shows the conceptions genuinely conflict — capital sentencing demands both constrained and unconstrained discretion — and argues that rigor consists in naming which failure-mode is at issue rather than invoking the bare epithet.
